Recall ladder · verbal only
03:30–05:00 · 1:30

Pick the first move.

Level 1

Which unit signals length, area, or volume?

What belongs in an average-speed denominator?

When does an inequality reverse direction?

Level 2

Percent change: multiplier chain or percent addition?

Missing mean: averages or a total ledger?

Two draws: one fraction or ordered paths?

“My next line will be…” Say a useful first line before doing arithmetic.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
05:00–07:30 · 2:30

Average speed keeps the waiting time.

01Level 4
A cyclist rides 12 km at 18 km/h, stops for 10 minutes, then rides 12 km back at 12 km/h. What is the average speed for the entire trip, in km/h?
A12
B14411
C15
D725

A useful lens

Speed is a fraction: total distance ÷ total elapsed time. The stop contributes time but no distance.

Ask before you calculate

Which times belong in the denominator? Are they all in the same unit?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
07:30–10:00 · 2:30

A new percent needs a new base.

02Level 4
A store increases an item’s original price by 25%, discounts the new price by 20%, then charges 8% sales tax. The customer pays $86.40. What was the original price?

A useful lens

Treat each percent as a multiplier door. To walk backward, divide by the combined multiplier; do not subtract the percents.

Ask before you calculate

What amount does each percent act on? Can you connect the original price to the final payment in one equation?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
10:00–12:30 · 2:30

Keep the order. Keep the sign.

03Level 2
Evaluate (−34 + 56) ÷ (−13) + 12. Give a fraction in simplest form.

A useful lens

Fence off the parentheses. Finish that calculation, then divide. The final addition comes last.

Ask before you calculate

Which operation comes first? What happens to the negative sign when you multiply by the reciprocal?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
12:30–15:00 · 2:30

Unpack, collect, isolate.

04Level 3
Solve 3(2x − 5) − 2(x + 4) = 5x − 29.

A useful lens

Distribute the sign with the number. Two short distribution lines are safer than one crowded mental jump.

Ask before you calculate

Does the −2 multiply both terms in its group? Can you verify your value in the original equation?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
15:00–17:30 · 2:30

The boundary is not the integer.

05Level 4
What is the smallest integer x satisfying −3(2x − 5) + 4 ≤ 2x + 2?

A useful lens

Solve the continuous inequality first. Only then obey the word “integer.” Test the nearest integer on each side.

Ask before you calculate

At what step could the order reverse? After finding a boundary, what must you still do?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
17:30–20:00 · 2:30

The unchanged group anchors the ratio.

06Level 4
A club has boys and girls in a ratio of 5:3. Eight girls join, and the new ratio of boys to girls is 5:4. How many members were in the club originally?

A useful lens

Anchor the boys. Their unchanged five parts let you compare old and new girl parts without inventing a new unit.

Ask before you calculate

Which group did not change? Can one equal-size block mean the same thing before and after?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
20:00–22:30 · 2:30

A shift moves. A stretch spreads.

07Level 3
The box plot shows travel times t, in minutes. Each is replaced by 32t − 3. What is the new interquartile range, in minutes?

A useful lens

IQR is the width of the box. Moving every observation shifts the box; multiplying every observation changes its width.

Ask before you calculate

Which two landmarks define IQR? What happens to the two subtraction terms when you take their difference?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
22:30–25:00 · 2:30

A mean is a total in disguise.

08Level 4
Twelve quizzes have a mean of 18 points; eight other quizzes have a mean of 15 points. One more quiz makes the mean of all 21 quizzes equal to 17 points. What is that last score?

A useful lens

Turn each mean back into a total. The missing score is the gap between the required total and the existing total.

Ask before you calculate

What total is already recorded? What total is required? Why is averaging 18 and 15 not a weighted mean?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
25:00–27:30 · 2:30

Trace the edge, not the picture.

09Level 4
A semicircular region has radius 7 cm. Which expressions equal its perimeter, in centimeters? Select all that apply.
A7π
B14 + 7π
C14π
D7(π + 2)

A useful lens

Half a circle gives half the curved circumference—not half the complete perimeter of the region.

Ask before you calculate

Where does a finger travel around the entire region? Which straight segment must you count?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
27:30–30:00 · 2:30

A corner can change area, not perimeter.

10Level 4
A 9 cm by 5 cm rectangle is removed from the lower-left corner of an 18 cm by 10 cm rectangle, as shown. What is the perimeter of the remaining region?

A useful lens

Imagine sliding the removed bottom and left edges inward. Compare the lengths lost with the lengths added before summing six segments.

Ask before you calculate

Which outer lengths disappear? Which new boundary lengths replace them?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
30:00–32:30 · 2:30

Uncube the multiplier first.

11Level 5
Two cubes are similar. The larger cube has 12564 times the smaller cube’s volume. Its surface area is 54 cm² greater than the smaller cube’s surface area. What is the smaller cube’s surface area?

A useful lens

Use a ratio ladder: volume → edge → area. The difference between two corresponding areas is not their ratio.

Ask before you calculate

How does a volume ratio become an edge ratio? How does that edge ratio become an area ratio?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Mixed sweep · 90 s attempt + 60 s explain
32:30–35:00 · 2:30

One color each has two orders.

12Level 3
A bag contains 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability of drawing one of each color?

A useful lens

Multiply along a path; add across different successful paths. Keep track of whether the first counter is returned.

Ask before you calculate

What changes after the first draw? Are R-then-B and B-then-R disjoint successful paths?
After committing: State the reusable rule in one sentence. Then focus on the next item.
Stretch A · scale, area, units
35:00–37:00 · 2:00

A box has a face inventory.

ALevel 5
A small closed display box measures 4 cm × 6 cm × 10 cm. A larger, similar box has 278 times its volume. The larger box is painted outside except for its bottom. One mL of paint covers 18 cm². How many mL are needed?

Start with the quantity type

Does the volume multiplier apply directly to an edge? To an area? What must you recover first?

Two traps to catch

A closed box still has a bottom. Paint coverage converts area to mL—not box volume to mL.
Stretch A · guided solution path 1 of 3
37:00–40:00 · 3:00

Recover the scale. Count the faces.

Step 1 · Recover a length multiplier

Let k multiply each edge. Then k³ = 278, so k = 32. The larger dimensions are 6 cm × 9 cm × 15 cm.

Step 2 · Inventory the painted area

The lid contributes one 6 × 9 rectangle. The four walls contribute two 6 × 15 and two 9 × 15 rectangles.

What did the net prevent?

Which face is left out? Why is there still one horizontal face to paint?
A = 6·9 + 2(6·15) + 2(9·15)
Stretch A · independent final calculation
40:00–42:00 · 2:00

Finish with the unit you need.

Step 3 · Convert area to paint

Divide the total painted area by the coverage rate. Keep the rate’s units visible.
Paint = 6·9 + 2(6·15) + 2(9·15)18 mL

Can you check another way?

Write the paintable area of the small box. Should multiplying by (3/2)² reproduce the larger painted area?

A useful shortcut

Similar surfaces scale with the square of the length multiplier—even when the same corresponding face is excluded.
Explain: Which factor scales lengths, which scales areas, and which converts units?
Stretch B · overlap and two draws
42:00–44:30 · 2:30

First choose the eligible crowd.

BLevel 5
Of 120 students, 68 join robotics, 54 join chess, and 18 join neither. Two different students are chosen at random from those in at least one club. What is the probability that one is robotics-only and the other is chess-only, in either order?

Listen for two restrictions

Who is eligible? Which eligible students cannot be part of a successful pair?

Keep the two jobs separate

“At least one” names the sample space. “Only” restricts successful outcomes.
Stretch B · guided solution path 2 of 3
44:30–47:30 · 3:00

Turn circles into separate groups.

Step 1 · Repair the double count

Eligible: 120 − 18 = 102 students.
The club totals count the overlap twice, so both clubs: 68 + 54 − 102 = 20.

Step 2 · Isolate exclusive groups

Robotics-only: 68 − 20 = 48.
Chess-only: 54 − 20 = 34.
The overlap remains eligible, but not successful.

Check the bookkeeping

Do the three inside regions add to the eligible total? Why do the 18 outside students disappear from the denominators?

Count before calculating probability

The original club totals still include students in both clubs. They cannot stand for the exclusive groups.
Stretch B · independent final calculation
47:30–50:00 · 2:30

Multiply along. Add across.

Step 3 · Build both successful orders

One order is robotics-only then chess-only; the other reverses them. Removing a student changes the second denominator.
P = 48102·34101 + 34102·48101

Where is the fast cancellation?

Can you factor out the repeated product? Which numerator is a factor of the first denominator?
Explain the structure: Why addition between paths, but multiplication within each path?
Stretch C · ratios, transfer, percent
50:00–52:00 · 2:00

The fraction travels with the liquid.

CLevel 5
Tank A holds 80 L of red and blue liquid in the ratio 3:2. Tank B holds 64 L in the ratio 1:3. Some well-mixed liquid moves from A to B. B’s new red-to-blue ratio is 2:3. What percentage of A’s original liquid was transferred?

Name the unknown precisely

If x liters move, what fraction of x is red? Which tank has the final ratio?

Two wholes do different jobs

The target composition uses B’s new total. The requested percent uses A’s original total.
Stretch C · guided solution path 3 of 3
52:00–55:00 · 3:00

Carry the composition into the equation.

Step 1 · Translate the starting contents

A: 80·(3/5) = 48 L red; 32 L blue.
B: 64·(1/4) = 16 L red; 48 L blue.

Step 2 · Follow the red liquid

Let x liters transfer. B receives (3/5)x liters of red liquid; B’s new total is 64 + x liters.

Why is the target not two-thirds?

A red-to-blue ratio of 2:3 has five total parts. What fraction of the new total must be red?
16 + 35x = 25(64 + x)

A moving-part shortcut

Track one color and the total, instead of writing separate equations for both colors.
Stretch C · independent final calculation
55:00–57:00 · 2:00

Solve liters. Then change the question.

Step 3 · Clear fractions, then convert

Multiply the equation by 5. Solve for liters transferred; only then express that amount as a percent of A’s original 80 L.
80 + 3x = 128 + 2x
Percentage = x80·100%

Does the model make physical sense?

Could x be negative or greater than 80 L? Should adding A’s redder mixture increase B’s red share?

One last base check

The number of liters is not the requested percent. Circle the original whole named in the question.
Confidence close · process, not prediction

Leave with a dependable move.

Name three moves you trust

Choose: total-time speed, percent multipliers, ratio parts, mean-as-total, boundary tracing, cubic scaling, or ordered paths.

One uncertain item is finished. My next job is to read the new question—not replay the last one.

Choose one process code

C: careless · M: misread · G: content gap
T: timing · S: strategy
Name one countermeasure, not a score prediction.

A complete check is small

Requested quantity? Correct units? Sensible size? Check before advancing.
